item.title: Reading Limits from a Described Graph and Oscillation
item.stimulus:
The graph of a function g on the interval −5 ≤ x ≤ 6 is described in words below. The graph has no other points.

• For −5 ≤ x < −2, the graph is a line segment from the filled point (−5, 1) to an open circle at (−2, 4).
• At x = −2, the only point on the graph is the filled point (−2, 0).
• For −2 < x < 1, the graph is a line segment from an open circle at (−2, 4) to an open circle at (1, −2).
• For 1 ≤ x < 3, the graph starts at the filled point (1, 3) and increases without bound as x approaches 3 from the left.
• g(3) is not defined, and the line x = 3 is a vertical asymptote.
• For 3 < x ≤ 6, the graph decreases from arbitrarily large values near x = 3 down to the filled point (6, 2).

Separately, let p(x) = sin(π/x) for x ≠ 0.
item.model_answer:
(a) The filled point at x = −2 is (−2, 0), so g(−2) = 0. From the left, the segment from (−5, 1) approaches the open circle at (−2, 4), so lim x→−2⁻ g(x) = 4. From the right, the segment approaches the same open circle, so lim x→−2⁺ g(x) = 4. Since both one-sided limits equal 4, lim x→−2 g(x) = 4, even though g(−2) = 0.

(b) To the left of 1, the segment approaches the open circle at (1, −2), so lim x→1⁻ g(x) = −2. To the right, the graph starts at the filled point (1, 3), so lim x→1⁺ g(x) = 3. Because −2 ≠ 3, the left-hand and right-hand limits are not equal, so lim x→1 g(x) does not exist.

(c) As x→3⁻, g(x) increases without bound, and as x→3⁺, g(x) also takes arbitrarily large values. So lim x→3⁻ g(x) = ∞ and lim x→3⁺ g(x) = ∞, and we write lim x→3 g(x) = ∞. This means g is unbounded near x = 3, so the limit does not exist as a finite number.

(d) p(1/n) = sin(π/(1/n)) = sin(nπ) = 0. p(2/(4n+1)) = sin(π(4n+1)/2) = sin(2nπ + π/2) = 1. Both 1/n and 2/(4n+1) are positive and approach 0 as n grows, so arbitrarily close to 0 on the right p takes the value 0 and also the value 1. The function oscillates and does not approach a single number, so lim x→0⁺ p(x) does not exist. The student is wrong; the plot sampled only points where p = 0 and missed the oscillation between them.

import sympy as sp
from fractions import Fraction
x=sp.symbols('x')
n=sp.symbols('n',integer=True,positive=True)
# segment from (-5,1) to (-2,4)
L1=1+(x+5)*Fraction(3,3)
assert sp.simplify(L1.subs(x,-2))==4
# segment from (-2,4) to (1,-2)
m=Fraction(-2-4,1-(-2))
L2=4+m*(x+2)
assert sp.simplify(L2.subs(x,-2))==4
assert sp.simplify(L2.subs(x,1))==-2
assert -2!=3
# part d
p=sp.sin(sp.pi/x)
for k in range(1,30):
    assert sp.simplify(p.subs(x,sp.Rational(1,k)))==0
    assert sp.simplify(p.subs(x,sp.Rational(2,4*k+1)))==1
assert sp.simplify(sp.sin(n*sp.pi))==0
assert sp.simplify(sp.sin((4*n+1)*sp.pi/2))==1
assert sp.limit(sp.Rational(1,1)/n,n,sp.oo)==0
assert sp.limit(2/(4*n+1),n,sp.oo)==0
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: A student plots p(x) = sin(π/x) using only the x-values 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, … . Every plotted point lies on the x-axis, so the student concludes that lim x→0⁺ p(x) = 0. For each positive integer n, compute p(1/n) and p(2/(4n+1)). Then explain whether the student's conclusion is correct.

criteria.text: Computes p(1/n) = sin(nπ) = 0 and p(2/(4n+1)) = sin((4n+1)π/2) = 1.
criteria.evidence: Both values are shown with the substitution into sin(π/x).
criteria.fix: Substitute the given x into π/x, simplify, then use that sin(nπ) = 0 and sin(π/2 + 2nπ) = 1.

criteria.evidence: Response notes both sequences of x-values approach 0 from the right yet p equals 0 on one and 1 on the other, so p oscillates and the limit does not exist; may mention the plot missed behavior between sampled points.
criteria.fix: A plot can miss behavior between sampled points; if outputs keep taking two different values arbitrarily close to a point, the limit does not exist.

item.title: Reading Limits from a Described Piecewise Graph
item.stimulus:
A function g is defined for -4 ≤ x ≤ 6 except at x = 4. Its graph is described in words below. A closed point is part of the graph. An open circle marks a point that is not on the graph.

1. For -4 ≤ x < -1, the graph is a straight line segment. It starts at the closed point (-4, 0) and ends at an open circle at (-1, 3).
2. At x = -1 there is a single closed point at (-1, 1), so g(-1) = 1.
3. For -1 < x < 2, the graph is a straight line segment. It runs from an open circle at (-1, -2) to an open circle at (2, 4).
4. At x = 2 there is a single closed point at (2, 0), so g(2) = 0.
5. For 2 < x < 4, the graph is an unbroken increasing curve. It starts at the open circle at (2, 4) and rises without bound as x approaches 4 from the left.
6. The vertical line x = 4 is a vertical asymptote, and g(4) is not defined.
7. For 4 < x ≤ 6, the graph is an unbroken decreasing curve. It comes down from arbitrarily large values just to the right of x = 4 and ends at the closed point (6, 1).
item.model_answer:
(a) As x → -1 from the left, the first segment approaches the open circle at (-1, 3), so lim x→-1⁻ g(x) = 3. As x → -1 from the right, the second segment approaches the open circle at (-1, -2), so lim x→-1⁺ g(x) = -2. Since 3 ≠ -2, the left-hand and right-hand limits are not equal. Therefore lim x→-1 g(x) does not exist. The closed point (-1, 1) does not affect this.

(b) From the left, the segment on (-1, 2) approaches the height 4 at x = 2. From the right, the curve on (2, 4) starts at the open circle (2, 4), so it also approaches 4. Both one-sided limits equal 4, so lim x→2 g(x) = 4. The closed point at (2, 0) gives g(2) = 0. These values can differ because a limit describes the values g(x) approaches as x gets close to 2, not the value of g at x = 2 itself.

(c) As x approaches 4 from the left, the graph rises without bound, so lim x→4⁻ g(x) = ∞. As x approaches 4 from the right, the graph comes down from arbitrarily large values, so lim x→4⁺ g(x) = ∞. Thus lim x→4 g(x) = ∞. This means g is unbounded near x = 4, so the limit does not exist as a real number.

(d) As x → -4 from the right, the first segment approaches its starting point (-4, 0), so lim x→-4⁺ g(x) = 0. As x → 6 from the left, the decreasing curve approaches (6, 1), so lim x→6⁻ g(x) = 1.
The limit fails to exist at exactly two values of c.
At c = -1, the one-sided limits are 3 and -2, which are unequal.
At c = 4, g is unbounded on both sides.
At c = 2, the limit exists and equals 4, even though g(2) = 0. Everywhere else in (-4, 6), the graph is an unbroken segment or curve, so the limit exists.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction as F

def seg(p, q):
    (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = p, q
    m = F(y2 - y1, x2 - x1)
    return lambda x: y1 + m * (x - x1)

s1 = seg((-4, 0), (-1, 3))
s2 = seg((-1, -2), (2, 4))

# part (a)
assert s1(-1) == 3
assert s2(-1) == -2
assert s1(-1) != s2(-1)

# part (b): left-hand limit at 2 is 4, and the right-hand curve starts at the open circle (2, 4)
assert s2(2) == 4
right_start = 4
assert s2(2) == right_start
g2 = 0
assert g2 != 4

# part (d)
assert s1(-4) == 0
end_value = 1
assert end_value == 1

# points where the limit fails: unequal one-sided limits or unbounded behavior
breaks = {-1: (s1(-1), s2(-1)), 2: (s2(2), right_start)}
fail = sorted([c for c, (l, r) in breaks.items() if l != r] + [4])
assert fail == [-1, 4]

print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Reading Limits from a Verbally Described Graph
item.stimulus:
The graph of a function g on the interval −4 ≤ x ≤ 5, x ≠ 3, is described in words below. An open circle means the point is not on the graph; a filled dot means the point is on the graph.

• For −4 ≤ x < −1, the graph is the line segment from the filled dot (−4, 0) to an open circle at (−1, 3).
• At x = −1, there is a filled dot at (−1, 1).
• For −1 < x < 2, the graph is the line segment from an open circle at (−1, −2) to an open circle at (2, 4).
• At x = 2, there is a filled dot at (2, 0).
• For 2 < x < 3, the graph starts at an open circle at (2, 4) and increases without bound as x approaches 3 from the left.
• For 3 < x ≤ 5, the graph increases without bound as x approaches 3 from the right, and it decreases to the filled dot (5, 1). The line x = 3 is a vertical asymptote, and g(3) is not defined.

A second function is k(x) = sin(π/x) for x > 0.
item.model_answer:
(a) Approaching −1 from the left, the graph follows the segment from (−4, 0) toward the open circle at (−1, 3), so lim x→−1⁻ g(x) = 3. Approaching from the right, the graph follows the segment from the open circle at (−1, −2), so lim x→−1⁺ g(x) = −2. Since 3 ≠ −2, the one-sided limits are not equal, so lim x→−1 g(x) does not exist. (The value g(−1) = 1 does not affect this.)

(b) From the left, the segment approaches the open circle at (2, 4); from the right, the graph starts at the open circle at (2, 4). Both one-sided limits equal 4, so lim x→2 g(x) = 4. The filled dot at (2, 0) gives g(2) = 0. They differ because a limit depends only on the values of g for x near 2, not on the value of g at x = 2 itself.

(c) As x→3⁻ and as x→3⁺, g(x) increases without bound, so lim x→3⁻ g(x) = ∞ and lim x→3⁺ g(x) = ∞, which we write as lim x→3 g(x) = ∞. Because g is unbounded near x = 3, there is no finite value L; the limit does not exist as a real number.

(d) At x = 2/5, k(2/5) = sin(5π/2) = 1, and at x = 2/3, k(2/3) = sin(3π/2) = −1. More generally k(2/(4n+1)) = 1 and k(2/(4n+3)) = −1 for every positive integer n, while k(1/n) = sin(nπ) = 0. So in every interval (0, δ) there are x-values where k equals 1, where it equals −1, and where it equals 0. The function oscillates between −1 and 1 infinitely often as x→0⁺, so it does not approach a single value, and lim x→0⁺ k(x) does not exist. The student's plot sampled only the zeros, so its scale missed the oscillation.

assert seg1(-4) == 0 and seg1(-1) == 3
# segment 2: (-1,-2) to (2,4): y = 2x

assert seg2(-1) == -2 and seg2(2) == 4
left_m1 = seg1(-1); right_m1 = seg2(-1)

assert lim2_left == lim2_right == 4

item.title: Reading One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits from a Described Graph
item.stimulus:
The function g is defined for all x with −5 < x < 6 except x = 4. Its graph is described in words below. An open circle means the point is not on the graph; a filled point means the point is on the graph.

• For −5 < x < −2, the graph is a line segment that rises from near the point (−5, 1) to an open circle at (−2, 4).
• For −2 ≤ x < 1, the graph is a smooth curve that starts at a filled point at (−2, 1) and rises to an open circle at (1, 3).
• At x = 1, there is a single filled point at (1, −1) that is not attached to any curve.
• For 1 < x < 4, the graph is a curve that starts at the open circle (1, 3). As x approaches 4 from the left, the curve increases without bound along the vertical line x = 4.
• For 4 < x < 6, as x approaches 4 from the right, the graph also increases without bound. Moving right, the curve decreases to near the point (6, 2).
item.model_answer:
(a) Approaching x = −2 from the left, the line segment heads to the open circle at (−2, 4), so lim x→−2⁻ g(x) = 4. Approaching from the right, the curve starts at the filled point (−2, 1), so lim x→−2⁺ g(x) = 1. Since the left-hand limit 4 does not equal the right-hand limit 1, lim x→−2 g(x) does not exist.

(b) From the left, the curve on −2 ≤ x < 1 rises toward (1, 3); from the right, the curve on 1 < x < 4 starts at the open circle (1, 3). Both one-sided limits equal 3, so lim x→1 g(x) = 3. The filled point gives g(1) = −1. The limit describes the values of g(x) for x close to, but not equal to, 1, so the isolated value g(1) = −1 has no effect on the limit.

(c) As x → 4⁻ and as x → 4⁺, g(x) increases without bound, so lim x→4 g(x) = ∞. The limit does not exist as a real number, because g is unbounded near x = 4 and does not approach any finite value.

item.title: Reading One-Sided and Two-Sided Limits from a Described Graph
item.stimulus:
The graph of a function f, defined for −5 < x < 6 with x ≠ 4, is described below in words. An open circle means the point is not on the graph; a closed circle means it is on the graph.

• For −5 < x < −2, the graph is a straight line segment from an open circle at (−5, 0) to an open circle at (−2, 3).
• For −2 ≤ x < 1, the graph is a straight line segment from a closed circle at (−2, −1) to an open circle at (1, 2).
• At x = 1, the graph has a single closed circle at (1, −2).
• For 1 < x ≤ 3, the graph is a straight line segment from an open circle at (1, 2) to a closed circle at (3, 0).
• For 3 < x < 4, the graph rises from (3, 0) and increases without bound as x approaches 4. The line x = 4 is a vertical asymptote.
• For 4 < x < 6, the graph comes down from arbitrarily large values near x = 4 and decreases toward an open circle at (6, 1).

A second function g is defined for all x ≠ 0. Its graph is described as follows: in every open interval containing x = 0, no matter how small, the graph of g oscillates between y = −1 and y = 1, reaching each of these values infinitely many times.
item.model_answer:
(a) As x approaches −2 from the left, the graph follows the segment ending at the open circle (−2, 3), so lim x→−2⁻ f(x) = 3. From the right, the graph starts at (−2, −1), so lim x→−2⁺ f(x) = −1. Since 3 ≠ −1, the one-sided limits are not equal, so lim x→−2 f(x) does not exist.

(b) From the left, the segment approaches the open circle (1, 2), and from the right the segment also approaches the open circle (1, 2). So lim x→1⁻ f(x) = lim x→1⁺ f(x) = 2, and lim x→1 f(x) = 2. The closed circle gives f(1) = −2. The limit depends only on the values of f(x) for x near 1, not at x = 1, so the isolated point (1, −2) does not change the limit.

(c) As x→4⁻, the graph increases without bound, so lim x→4⁻ f(x) = ∞. As x→4⁺, the graph also comes down from arbitrarily large values, so lim x→4⁺ f(x) = ∞. Because f(x) is unbounded near x = 4, f(x) does not approach any real number, so lim x→4 f(x) does not exist as a real number (it can be described as lim x→4 f(x) = ∞).

(d) In every interval around x = 0, g(x) oscillates between −1 and 1, taking both values infinitely often. So g(x) does not get close to any single number as x→0, and lim x→0 g(x) does not exist.
item.verification_python:
import sympy as sp
x=sp.symbols('x')
def line(p,q):
    m=sp.Rational(q[1]-p[1],q[0]-p[0])
    return p[1]+m*(x-p[0])
A=line((-5,0),(-2,3))
B=line((-2,-1),(1,2))
C=line((1,2),(3,0))
assert A.subs(x,-5)==0 and A.subs(x,-2)==3
assert sp.limit(A,x,-2,'-')==3
assert sp.limit(B,x,-2,'+')==-1
assert B.subs(x,-2)==-1
assert sp.limit(A,x,-2,'-')!=sp.limit(B,x,-2,'+')
assert sp.limit(B,x,1,'-')==2
assert sp.limit(C,x,1,'+')==2
assert C.subs(x,3)==0
f1=-2
assert f1!=2
# model for asymptote behavior: 1/(x-4)^2 type growth
h=1/(x-4)**2
assert sp.limit(h,x,4,'-')==sp.oo and sp.limit(h,x,4,'+')==sp.oo
# oscillation: sin(1/x) takes 1 and -1 at points approaching 0
import math
for k in range(1,6):
    a=1/(math.pi/2+2*math.pi*k); b=1/(3*math.pi/2+2*math.pi*k)
    assert abs(math.sin(1/a)-1)<1e-9 and abs(math.sin(1/b)+1)<1e-9
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
